newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish interest rate cut seen in H2 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Polish interest rate cut seen in H2 - analysts.

text.p: Poland's official interest rates are expected to stay unchanged until at least the middle of 1997 when the central bank could lower them if price and credit growth slows, analysts said on Thursday.

"Official rates could be trimmed in the second half of 1997 unless inflation jumps, with a rate move more likely earlier rather than later," said Krzysztof Bledowski, chief economist at WoodCommerz in Warsaw.

Other analysts said the next adjustment in official rates, now at 22 and 25 percent, would take place around September, when results of this year's grain harvest would better indicate whether food prices would grow quickly at the end of the year.
Analysts agreed that rate moves would depend on whether troublesome growth of credit action was sufficiently curbed through the National Bank of Poland tight monetary policy.
Since December the NBP pulled up market rates and increased obligatory reserves on banks to cool domestic demand, which fuels imports and may further widen the trade deficit.

Pesonal credit, closely monitored by the central bank as an indicator of domestic demand, showed some signs of slowing in the first two months of 1997, but still grew 5.7 percent versus a 1.8 percent growth of broad money during that period.
Credit to households soared 108 percent in 1996.
Analysts' views echoed a statement given by Finance Minister Marek Belka earlier on Thursday.

"A real interest rate rise, which is happening because nominal rates are not being lowered, is justified...but later in the year, in the second half or in several months (official interest rate) cuts could take place, should take place and probably will take place," Belka said.
Analysts said that Belka's statement may have signalled that the treasury would not likely further increase yields on its short-term treasuries because of future rate cuts. @

"The treasury has had difficulties selling debt over the last month so Belka may have talked about a rate cut because he wanted to cap yields at present levels and stir up demand in bills," said one analyst at a foreign firm in Warsaw.
Analysts said that a small possibility of an official interest rate rise still existed, but they said that falling inflation would likely keep such a scenario from happening.

"It is very unlikely that the central bank will increase official rates because there is no basis for such a move," said Andrzej Kopec, chief dealer at Bank Slaski SA, adding that he expected an interest rate cut early in the second half. @

A monthly Reuter poll showed this week banks expected inflation, at year-on-year 18.1 percent in January, to fall to around 16.3 percent by the end of the year, above the official target of 13 percent.
